## Preamble

This script covers the `DESeq2` differential gene expression analysis for our samples.

## 1. Load Libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(DESeq2)
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
```

## 2. Load Data

One data frame per sample replicate, naming as follows:

- dpi<dpi-group>\_<infection-group>\_<sex><sample-number>\_rep<replicate-number>
  - e.g., dpi4_mock_m1_rep1

### 2.1 4 Days Post Infection Samples

```{r}
# Control (mock-infected) Samples
dpi4_mock_m1_rep1 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/14_S4_M_mock/ERR14210197_genecounts.out.tab",
                              col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                              skip = 4)
dpi4_mock_m1_rep2 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/14_S4_M_mock/ERR14210198_genecounts.out.tab",
                              col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                              skip = 4)
dpi4_mock_m1_rep3 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/14_S4_M_mock/ERR14210199_genecounts.out.tab",
                              col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                              skip = 4)

# SARS-CoV-2 Infected Samples
dpi4_cov_m1_rep1 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/137_S26_M_cov/ERR14210176_genecounts.out.tab",
                             col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                             skip = 4)
dpi4_cov_m1_rep2 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/137_S26_M_cov/ERR14210177_genecounts.out.tab",
                             col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                             skip = 4)
dpi4_cov_m1_rep3 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/4dpi_samples/137_S26_M_cov/ERR14210178_genecounts.out.tab",
                             col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                             skip = 4)
```

### 2.2 80 Days Post Infection Samples

```{r}
# Control (mock-infected) Samples
dpi80_mock_m1_rep1 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/80dpi_samples/mocksal_M1/ERR14210224_genecounts.out.tab",
                               col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                               skip = 4)
dpi80_mock_m1_rep2 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/80dpi_samples/mocksal_M1/ERR14210225_genecounts.out.tab",
                               col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                               skip = 4)

# SARS-CoV-2 Infected Samples
dpi80_cov_m1_rep1 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/80dpi_samples/covsal_M1/ERR14210240_genecounts.out.tab",
                              col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                              skip = 4)
dpi80_cov_m1_rep2 <- read_tsv("gene_counts/80dpi_samples/covsal_M1/ERR14210241_genecounts.out.tab",
                              col_names = c("gene_id", "total", "antisense", "sense"),
                              skip = 4)
```

## 3. Merge All Samples into Single Matrix

```{r}
data_matrix <- dpi4_mock_m1_rep1 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_mock_m1_rep1 = sense) %>%
  inner_join(dpi4_mock_m1_rep2 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_mock_m1_rep2 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi4_mock_m1_rep3 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_mock_m1_rep3 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi4_cov_m1_rep1 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_cov_m1_rep1 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi4_cov_m1_rep2 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_cov_m1_rep2 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi4_cov_m1_rep3 %>% select(gene_id, dpi4_cov_m1_rep3 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi80_mock_m1_rep1 %>% select(gene_id, dpi80_mock_m1_rep1 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi80_mock_m1_rep2 %>% select(gene_id, dpi80_mock_m1_rep2 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi80_cov_m1_rep1 %>% select(gene_id, dpi80_cov_m1_rep1 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  inner_join(dpi80_cov_m1_rep2 %>% select(gene_id, dpi80_cov_m1_rep2 = sense), by = "gene_id") %>%
  as.matrix()

head(data_matrix)
```

For compiling the metadata, so long as all the names follow a common naming convention, can just use the column names as strings and split on '\_' to get the different metadata points (i.e., dpi group, infected vs. control, sex (by "starts with m" and "starts with f"), and sample ("m1" is male sample 1... except might have issues with cross dpi m1 given that m1 dpi4 is not same as m1 dpi80...)).

## 4. Generate Metadata File

```{r}
sample_names <- colnames(data_matrix)
sample_names <- sample_names[2:length(sample_names)]

raw_metadata <- str_split(sample_names, "_")

# Note that the value for each subsequent column will only be unique by observation
# for all entries with the same values for *all* preceding columns.
# For example, replicate 1 will be duplicated for unique combinations of all other fields.
raw_metadata <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, raw_metadata),
                              row.names = colnames(data_matrix),
                              optional = FALSE,
                              cut.names = FALSE,
                              col.names = c("dpi", "condition", "sex", "sample", "rep"),
                              new.names = !missing(col.names),
                              check.names = !optional,
                              stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# ^^ This still doesn't work quite right just FYI.
```

#### BELOW HERE IS OLD FROM TUTORIAL 7 FILE

We need to set up a `metadata` file whose rownames match the **name** and the **order** of the columns of our matrix above! You can use Excel to create the metadata file, or use the `data.frame()` function in R.

```{r}
# Make our Metadata file that contains our column information for our matrix
metadata <- data.frame(row.names = colnames(dat_matrix), 
                       condition = c("1_hour", "1_hour", "12_hour", "12_hour"))
metadata
```

To make sure that the row names from our `metadata` file match the column names of our `matrix`, we can run the following code

```{r}
colnames(dat_matrix) == rownames(metadata)
```

We are ready to put our data into DESeq2!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Running DESeq2

DESeq2 requires that all of your data be in the shape of a `SummarizedExperiment` object. Since reshaping your input data with your code would be complicated, there are functions within DESeq2 specific for the source of your counts file, which will prepare your data for use in DESeq2. The function we need is called `DESeqDataSetFromMatrix()`. The required arguments for this function are: \* `countData`, which must provide a `matrix` with our raw count reads, \* `colData`, the independent variables you changed in your experiment (e.g. sex, treatment, tissue). Which we stored in our `metadata` object. \* `design`, The design argument is a formula designated by the tilde symbol `~` and identifies which independent variable(s) you want to investigate. In our data, we have only a single independent variable, i.e. `condition`. Experiments with multifactorial experimental design are a lot more complicated to investigate.

```{r deseq-dataset, warning = FALSE}
# Create our DESeq2 object
dds_matrix <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = dat_matrix, #matrix 
                              colData = metadata, #metadata file
                              design = ~condition)
# Lets look at the object we created
dds_matrix
```

In a DESeq2 data set, the design variables are stored as a **factor** (a data type in R), which by default are organized alphabetically (Factors are important ways to categorize and store data in R). Without further information, DESeq2 will use the condition that comes **first** alphabetically as reference or the control. If you were using `"treated"` and `"untreated"`, for example, DESeq2 would incorrectly assume that the `"treated"` samples are the **reference**. To prevent any confusion, we can set the name used as reference explicitly with the argument `ref` inside the `relevel()` function.

```{r set-controls}
# Set control condition using the relevel function, with 1 hour as the 'reference' level
dds_matrix$condition <- relevel(dds_matrix$condition, ref = "1_hour")

# Check the levels of dds_matrix$condition
levels(dds_matrix$condition)
```

Now that the reference level has been set, we can run DESeq2 on the dataset.

```{r deseq2, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
dds <- DESeq(dds_matrix)
```

It's also a good idea to save your DESeqDataSet object so you don't have to redo this analysis if you want to re-explore your data. You can do this by saving the `dds` object into a `.rds` file, which is just a binary R file.

```{r saveRDS}
saveRDS(dds, "dds.rds")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sanity Checks and Quality Assessment: Sample Clustering

Because the distribution of RNA Seq data is highly skewed, with a few highly expressed genes and many lowly expressed genes, it is often necessary to transform our data to visualize clustering (the purpose of this is to uncouple the variance of our data from the mean which violates assumptions of many downstream statistical tests). DESeq2 comes with the function `rlog()`, which log-transforms your count data (similarly, the `vst` function also transforms our data in a "log-like" fashion and is what I usually use for downstream clustering or visualization). After transformation, we can use PCA to identify which samples are more similar and if they group by one or more of the independent variables (in our case, we have only a single variable that can take "control" or "treated").

```{r pca}
# Perform log transformation on our count data
rld <- rlog(dds)

# Generate a PCA plot with DESeq2's plotPCA function
plotPCA(rld, intgroup = "condition") + coord_cartesian() 
```

A distance matrix is another way to examine how samples cluster. The code chunk below calculates distances between each sample and then maps a colour palette (defined with `colorRampPalette`) onto it so that more similar samples display darker colours.

```{r distance-matrix}
# Calculate distances between samples in our log-transformed data
sample_dists <- dist(t(assay(rld)))

# Convert the output to a matrix
sample_dist_matrix <- as.matrix(sample_dists)

# Remove the column names of our matrix
colnames(sample_dist_matrix) <- NULL

# Set the colour palette for our heatmap
colours <- colorRampPalette(rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")))(255)

# Generate a heatmap using the pheatmap package
pheatmap(sample_dist_matrix,
         clustering_distance_rows = sample_dists,
         clustering_distance_cols = sample_dists, 
         col = colours)
```

We see that the samples cluster together by condition and this is what we would expect! If the samples don't cluster together like you would expect them to, check for batch effects.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Extracting data from our DESeqDataSet object

Since our samples cluster according to the independent variable, we can move forward with our analysis. To examine our results, we can save them to our global environment. DESeq2 calculates results for all combinations of levels in your experimental design (pairwise comparisons for all levels). The `resultsNames()` function tells us the name of each result that DESeq2 has calculated, so we can choose which one to look at by specifying "name = " in `results()`. The `results()` function will output a matrix of all genes, including those with similar or differential expression between the two conditions.

```{r generate-result-table}
# Names of the results that DESeq2 calculated
resultsNames(dds)

# Now we will extract the results for our comparison between the 12h timepoint and the 1h timepoint
res <- results(dds, name = "condition_12_hour_vs_1_hour") %>% as.data.frame() # we save it as a dataframe for easy manipulation with dplyr 
head(res)
```

**Note:** If you have multiple comparisons in your data (e.g. 1h, 6h, 12h), you can extract specific comparisons using the `results()` function combined with the `contrast =` argument. The contrast argument accepts a vector of length 3 where the first item is the factor/comparison, the second is the numerator (treatment), and the third is the denominator (control). Both the numerator and denominator must be levels of the factor you're investigating. For example, if you wanted to extract a matrix comparing gene expression at 12h compared to 6h, you could use the following code:

```{r generate-results-table_contrast, eval = FALSE}
results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "12h", "6h"))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data manipulation and "wrangling" with `dplyr`

Let's start by checking taking a *glimpse* of our data. The `glimpse()` function outputs a short summary of your dataframe including the number of rows, columns, and each column. Pay attention to the row number, we will be keeping track of how many observation we filter out at each step!

```{r}
glimpse(res)
```

Let's view our results!

```{r}
view(res)
```

You see that some column have "NA" values, this can happen for the following reasons: \* If within a row, all samples have zero counts, the baseMean column will be zero, and the log2 fold change estimates, p value and adjusted p-value will all be set to NA.

- If a row contains a sample with an extreme count outlier then the p value and adjusted p-value will be set to NA. These outlier counts are detected by Cook's distance.

- If a row is filtered by automatic independent filtering, for having a low mean normalized count, then only the adjusted p-value will be set to NA.

<br></br>

Lets use dplyr package to get rid of the rows with the NA values, as they have biased or not useful information. We will use the dplyr `drop_na()` function to filter out any row with an NA value

```{r}
res_no_NA <- res %>% drop_na()

# How many rows did we filter out!? --> about 2200.
glimpse(res_no_NA) 
```

Since we are only interested in differentially expressed genes, we can use `dplyr` functions to keep results with an adjusted *p*-value \< 0.05. Lets use the `filter()` function.

```{r}
res_filtered <- res_no_NA %>% 
  filter(padj <= 0.05)

# How many rows did we filter out!? --> 5682 compared to no NA data frame.
glimpse(res_filtered)
```

Generally, a gene that has **2X** higher/lower expression is considered 'biologically relevant'. We can also filter the data to pin-point these genes:

```{r}
res_filtered_final <- res_filtered %>% 
  filter(abs(log2FoldChange) >= 1) %>% # the '|' stand for OR here!
  rownames_to_column("gene_id") # Convert the rownames into a column so they can be saved in your CSV file

head(res_filtered_final)
```

**NOTE** you could have used `%>%` to do all of these filtering steps into one line. Give this a try!!

`dplyr` is also useful to explore your data. Say we wanted to see the top 10 genes that were the most differentially expressed. We can use the `arrange()` function to achieve this.

```{r}
# Top 10 upregulated genes (most positive log2FoldChange)
top10_genes <- res_filtered_final %>%
  arrange(desc(log2FoldChange)) %>% # NOTE that we use the desc() function to organize the column in descending order
  head(n = 10)
top10_genes

# Top 10 downregulated genes (most negative log2FoldChange)
bot10_genes <- res_filtered_final %>%
  arrange(log2FoldChange) %>% # NOTE since we don't use desc(), the column is organized in ascending order
  head(n = 10)
bot10_genes
```

Finally, lets save our filtered results into a file that we can open up with Excel. We will use the `write_csv()` function

```{r}
write_csv(res_filtered_final, "chlamy_results.csv")
```

**NOTE:** You need to include the `rownames_to_columns("gene_id")` line of code when creating the `res_filtered_final` object so that the rownames are stored in your CSV file!
